title: Multimodal Time Series Anomaly Detection with Semantic Alignment
one_liner: Catch anomalies in sensor data by reading the numbers together with the text descriptions that explain what is happening.
lead: Real-world systems like power grids or manufacturing equipment produce time series—streams of numbers recorded over time—but they also come with text descriptions: log files, notes from operators, maintenance records. Today's anomaly detection (finding when something has gone wrong) only looks at the numbers, ignoring the text entirely. This paper proposes MindTS, a model that reads both the numbers and the text at once, aligns their meanings, and learns which signals matter by filtering out the noise in the text. The result is more reliable anomaly detection because the model now understands the context in which readings occur—it can tell whether an unusual number is explained by something benign (scheduled maintenance) or is truly an alarm.

problem.h2: Anomaly detection on numbers alone misses the context
paras: A power plant records thousands of sensor readings every minute—temperature, pressure, flow rate. An anomaly detector (a model trained to recognize when something is wrong) looks at these numbers and learns what normal looks like, then flags readings that are very different. But the plant also keeps text logs: operator notes, equipment maintenance records, weather alerts. These logs often explain WHY a reading is the way it is.

The naive approach reads only the numbers, so it cannot distinguish between a reading that is odd but explained (a sensor gave a weird value because it was recalibrated this morning) and a reading that is truly dangerous (the same weird value with no explanation). The model wastes effort on false alarms and misses real problems that happen to have text clues in the logs.

callout.html: A single stream of numbers cannot capture the full story when text descriptions are available.

steps.b: Read the numbers and text together
steps.text: For each time step, both the sensor reading and the corresponding text description enter the model.
The model learns to match concepts from the text with patterns in the numbers—e.g., the text mentions maintenance, the numbers show expected drift.

A content condenser throws away text that does not help explain the numbers, keeping only the informative parts, because including irrelevant text would confuse the anomaly detector and raise false-alarm rates.

The filtered text modality and the numbers are merged via cross-modal reconstruction, so the model learns from both at once, because jointly training on both signals lets them correct each other—numbers constrain text interpretation, and text guides number interpretation.
The combined signal is scored: high scores flag readings the model thinks are anomalous.

paras: Normally, anomaly detection looks at numbers only. MindTS adds a second path: it reads the text and learns to say which parts of the text explain which parts of the number stream. It then uses this alignment to decide which text signals to keep and which to discard, so the fusion of numbers and text is based on real explanation, not noise.

hidden.name: semantic coherence (how well text explains the numbers)
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: for each time step, how coherent is the text with the number readings? A high coherence score means the text provides a good explanation for what the numbers show. Low coherence means the text is noise or irrelevant.

The model learns this by training a cross-modal alignment mechanism: it compares the text embeddings (a list of numbers representing the meaning of the text) with patterns in the sensor readings, scoring their agreement. This score is then used by the content condenser to keep only the high-coherence text signals when fusing the two modalities.

heat.caption: Darker means the text at that step has high coherence with the sensor data.

reads.html: Some text notes explain the numbers; others are noise. The model learns which is which by measuring how well the text aligns with what the numbers are doing.
Fine-grained semantic alignment scores the correspondence between text embeddings and multimodal representations; content condenser uses this to gate the text modality.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: two modalities correcting each other
paras: The trick is that numbers and text have different strengths. A number stream can capture what is happening (a pressure spike) but not why. Text can capture the context (a filter was replaced today) but is sparse and might miss fine timing. By measuring how well the text semantically aligns with the numbers, the model learns to use text as a guide to interpret the numbers and to ignore text that does not align—cutting out noise.

When text has high coherence with the numbers, the model learns to trust it and let it influence the anomaly score. When text is incoherent (the log says pressure is steady but the number spikes), the model learns to suppress it. Cross-modal reconstruction forces the two streams to co-adapt: the numbers learn to be explained by the text, and the text learns which details matter to the numbers. The result is a richer signal: anomalies are easier to spot because the model now knows the context in which they occur.

stages.s: Extract meaning from text; align to number patterns
Score how well text explains the numbers
Filter out low-coherence text; keep only explanatory signals
Fuse filtered text with numbers via cross-modal reconstruction

math.h2: The formula for semantic alignment and filtering
math.words: The anomaly score is the sum of the weighted number readings plus the cross-modal term. The weight for each text signal is based on how well it aligns with the number stream; low-alignment signals are suppressed. When text and numbers agree, the fusion term amplifies the signal; when they disagree, it dampens it.
math.equation: anomaly_score = sum_i (x_i) + lambda * sum_j (align_j * text_j * x_j)
symbols: the value of sensor i at this time step
semantic alignment score for text signal j (higher means text explains the numbers better)
the content of text signal j (encoded as a number)
strength of the cross-modal term; higher means text influences the decision more

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Time step t: sensor readings x1=2.5 (temp), x2=3.1 (pressure).
Text: Pump serviced. Alignment score align_j=0.8 (text explains the readings well).
Cross-modal term: lambda=0.5, text_j=1.2, so 0.5 * 0.8 * 1.2 * 2.5 = 1.2 boost.
With alignment: 5.6 + 1.2 = 6.8. But if align_j=0.1 (text does not explain readings): 5.6 + 0.5 * 0.1 * 1.2 * 2.5 = 5.75 (almost no change). Low-alignment text is filtered out.

math.note: The alignment score acts as a gate: only text that semantically explains the numbers gets to influence the final anomaly decision.

bars.h2: How much better does it get?

charts.title: Numbers only (baseline)
charts.note: The model misses context, so it flags many false alarms and misses some real anomalies.

charts.title: MindTS (with text alignment)
charts.note: Text provides context, semantic alignment filters noise, cross-modal fusion raises recall and precision together.

items.html: If the alignment mechanism is poorly trained, it might give high coherence scores to text that does not actually explain the numbers. The model then trusts the wrong signals, and anomaly detection gets worse. Fix: train the alignment module with a clear objective that measures how well text and numbers actually correlate.

If the text logs are sparse (many time steps with no text, or just generic notes), the model has little to align with the numbers. The cross-modal term vanishes, and performance reverts to the baseline. The method works best when text is dense and informative.

items.b: The content condenser throws away useful signals.
items.html: If the condenser is too aggressive (filters out too much text), the fusion loses valuable information. If it is too lenient (keeps all text), the model is back to reading noisy text. The balance depends on how much text is actually related to anomalies in this dataset.

items.b: Done right: text and numbers improve each other.
items.html: Train the alignment module end-to-end so it learns which text signals correlate with number patterns. Validate the condenser by measuring how many true anomalies are explained by the retained text. Tune lambda so that text has the right strength—neither overwhelming the numbers nor disappearing into the background. Test on data where text is dense and relevant.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic multimodal dataset: time series (e.g., 3-4 sensor streams) and paired text descriptions for a fraction of the time steps. Embed the text (using a standard text encoder like BERT, which turns words into numbers), train MindTS end-to-end, and compare its anomaly scores against a baseline that reads only the numbers. Run the content condenser to show which text signals are kept and which are filtered out. Plot the kept signals against the sensor anomalies to visually verify that semantic alignment is working: text that is kept should correlate with anomalies.
demo.metric_eq: precision = correct_anomalies / (correct_anomalies + false_alarms); recall = correct_anomalies / (correct_anomalies + missed_anomalies); F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)
demo.closing: The demo must show that (1) semantic alignment successfully separates useful text from noise, (2) the fused model's F1 score beats the number-only baseline, and (3) the patterns of kept text make intuitive sense (e.g., maintenance notes align with pressure readings).
